Tom.review: Butterfly is great, and one body line from the start is right. The problem is the angles. The long horizontal line across the middle and the lower wings leave the body at nearly sideways, so they'd never get the fall. The upper wings leave at roughly 45-50 degrees, which is borderline, so tighten them. Please redraw so every wing line leaves the body going up-and-out at 30-35 degrees at most, then curves out and round. Drop the straight cross bar. Do the lower wings as a branch lower down the body, also leaving up-and-out gently, then curving down around the lower wing and back in. Keep the wings as big smooth loops, no tiny strokes. Antennae are fine as gentle branches off the top of the body.

Priya.say: Love the butterfly, Leo, nice and symmetrical. Engineering notes, mostly about angles. The flat line that goes straight across the body, and the lower wings leaving the body sideways, are the big ones: the fall runs up the body, so anything leaving at close to a right angle just won't get knocked. Can we have each wing edge leave the body angling upward, not much more than about forty degrees off the body, then curve out and round? For the lower wings, start them lower on the body and sweep them up and out, then loop down and back in. Also soften the pointy corners on the wings into rounder curves, since a sharp turn breaks the chain. Antennae look fine. Upper wing diagonals are borderline, so make them a little steeper. Once you redraw, I'll dry-run it before we lock.
Priya.thinking: Reviewing Leo's draft as Eng. Main issues: the horizontal lines across the body and the lower wing edges leave the body at about 90 degrees, so they'd never fall. Also the corners are sharp, so round them. Antennae and upper wing diagonals are OK-ish.

recap:
The client wanted something colourful that flies and visits flowers, with no birds. Maya chose a butterfly, Leo drafted it, and Tom and Priya tightened the wings so every piece would join the outline.

Maya laid the body and antennae, and Leo took the lower wings. Then the upper wings became a tangle. Several people started the same ones. "If we both do it we'll lift each other's dominoes," Priya warned. Her dry run showed the upper wings never caught, because they left the body too sideways.

Tom sketched steeper replacements that climbed the body before bowing out. Maya traced the right wing, and Leo the left. Leo's inner end sat on the wrong line, but Tom reported it still caught through the lower line. Maya laid the last piece as the clock ran down.
